explain.say: Almost every school book shows the same pyramid: a king at the top, then lords, then knights, then peasants at the bottom. It is called feudalism. But here is a surprise: nobody in the Middle Ages used that word. It was invented by lawyers and writers in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Look at the pyramid on the board.

explain.say: In the classic model, the king grants land, a fief, to a lord, his vassal, who swears loyalty and supplies knights. The lord grants smaller fiefs to knights in turn. Look at the bottom layer, the biggest: peasants and serfs, who owed labour and rent to the lord of the manor. Historians call that second system manorialism. Can you see why the pyramid is so neat?

explain.say: Now the debate. In 1974 Elizabeth A. R. Brown called feudalism a tyranny of a construct, an idea that forces messy evidence into one shape. In 1994 Susan Reynolds's Fiefs and Vassals argued that the formal fief came late, often from university lawyers, not from early medieval practice. Why might a neat model mislead us?

explain.say: Feudal has travelled far. Look at the map. Historians have used it for samurai Japan and, in R. S. Sharma's Indian Feudalism, 1965, for early medieval India. Marxists use feudal for a whole way of producing based on lords and peasants. Is it fair to use one European word for all these societies?

Most medievalists now avoid the pyramid and describe lordship, land, kinship and law region by region. Others keep feudal as a loose shorthand. Fantastic thinking. Exam tip: if you use the word, define it in your first paragraph and name Brown or Reynolds.

faq.a: In the classic model, a system in medieval Europe where kings and lords granted land, called fiefs, to vassals in exchange for loyalty and military service, resting on peasants who worked the land. Many historians now question the model.
asks: What did a king give to his lords?

faq.a: Relationships of lordship, land and service certainly existed, but critics like Elizabeth Brown and Susan Reynolds argue that a single feudal system did not, and that the word distorts how varied medieval societies were.

faq.q: What did Susan Reynolds argue about fiefs and vassals?
faq.a: In Fiefs and Vassals, 1994, Reynolds argued that the precise fief and vassal relationship of textbooks was largely a creation of later medieval lawyers and modern historians, not the basis of early medieval society.
Not medieval people. Lawyers and scholars of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, writing about feudal law and the fief, from Latin feudum, built the idea of a feudal system.
asks: When was the word feudal first used?

faq.q: What is the difference between feudalism and manorialism?
faq.a: Feudalism, in the narrow sense, concerns relations between lords and their armed vassals. Manorialism describes the economic relationship between a lord and the peasants and serfs who worked his estate.

facts: Elizabeth A. R. Brown's article The Tyranny of a Construct appeared in the American Historical Review in 1974.
Susan Reynolds published Fiefs and Vassals in 1994.
Marc Bloch's Feudal Society was published in two volumes in 1939 and 1940.
